result:
I graded `s2` and saved the results, with feedback for each answer, to `grades/0001-s2.json`. I tried to run a check that the file parses as JSON, but the command needed approval and didn't run.

| Item | Verdict | In short |
|---|---|---|
| q1 | Correct | The loop is what makes it an agent. |
| q2 | Correct | The model outputs a request to use a tool. |
| q3 | Wrong (M6: no stopping condition) | A repeating agent needs a step limit, not more time. |
| q4 | Partial (M4: model runs tools) | 4 is right, but your program runs the tools, not the model. |
| q5 | Correct | You explained that the result goes back to the model, and why. |
| q6 | Partial | The model uses each tool's description and parameters (its inputs) as well as its name. |

**Summary:** you understand the basic loop, and you explained well what happens to a tool's result. Work first on **who does what**: the model asks for a tool, and your program runs it. You picked the right answer on this in q2, but your reason in q4 said the opposite. This matters for your design, because your team's code is what actually checks the calendar and books equipment time. Also review stopping conditions (q3) and how the model chooses a tool (q6).

**Next step:** without looking back, trace the laser cutter request from q4 in two columns, "model" and "program". Put every request, tool run and result in order, then mark where the program would check a step limit. Send it to me here and we'll go through it before moving on to context and memory.

I also added two learning records, one for what you showed on q5 and one for the open q4 mix-up, and updated `NOTES.md`. I didn't grade your first attempt, `s1`, because you only asked for `s2`. I can grade it too if you'd like.
